claim: VirSorter identified 12,498 high-confidence viral sequences from 14,977 publicly available bacterial and archaeal genomic data sets.
source: Applied to 14,977 publicly available microbial genomes (Figure 1—source data 1), VirSorter identified 12,498 high-confidence viral sequences representing either long genome fragments (>10 kb when linear) or complete genomes (contigs detected as circular).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of sequences identified by VirSorter from the analyzed genomes.

claim: The VirSorter curated data set augments public viral data sets approximately 10-fold.
source: This identified 12,498 high-confidence viral sequences with known hosts, ∼10-fold more than in the RefSeqVirus database, that we then used to expand our understanding of viral diversity and virus–host interactions.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the fold-increase compared to RefSeqVirus database.

claim: Viral sequences were found in approximately 30% of the microbial genomes analyzed.
source: These viral sequences were found in 5492 of the microbial genomes (∼30%).
evidence: The manuscript provides the specific number and percentage of genomes containing viral sequences.

claim: The study provides first viral sequences for 13 new bacterial phyla including ecologically abundant phyla.
source: These data augment public data sets 10-fold, provide first viral sequences for 13 new bacterial phyla including ecologically abundant phyla, and help taxonomically identify 7–38% of 'unknown' sequence space in viromes.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the number of new phyla for which viral sequences were identified.

claim: The VirSorter curated data set helps taxonomically identify 7-38% of 'unknown' sequence space in viromes.
source: These data augment public data sets 10-fold, provide first viral sequences for 13 new bacterial phyla including ecologically abundant phyla, and help taxonomically identify 7–38% of 'unknown' sequence space in viromes.
evidence: The abstract provides the specific range of improvement in virome affiliation.

claim: 264 new viral genera were identified, doubling the number of known genera.
source: Genome- and network-based classification was largely consistent with accepted viral taxonomy and suggested that (i) 264 new viral genera were identified (doubling known genera) and (ii) cross-taxon genomic recombination is limited.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the number of new genera identified and their relationship to previously known genera.

claim: 90.45% of the 12,498 sequences correspond to Caudovirales.
source: BLAST-based family-level affiliations suggested that 90.45% of these 12,498 sequences correspond to Caudovirales, 6.82% to ssDNA viruses (predominantly Inoviridae family), and 2.73% could not be confidently assigned (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages based on BLAST-based affiliations, with supporting figure.

claim: 6.82% of the sequences correspond to ssDNA viruses, predominantly Inoviridae family.
source: BLAST-based family-level affiliations suggested that 90.45% of these 12,498 sequences correspond to Caudovirales, 6.82% to ssDNA viruses (predominantly Inoviridae family), and 2.73% could not be confidently assigned (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages for ssDNA virus representation.

claim: More than 25,000 bacterial and archaeal host genomes are available in NCBI RefSeq as of January 2015.
source: This is because the lack of a universal marker gene for viruses hinders environmental survey capabilities, while the number of isolate viral genomes in databases remains limited: for comparison, more than 25,000 bacterial and archaeal host genomes are available in NCBI RefSeq (January 2015), whereas only 1,531 of their viruses were entirely sequenced and most (86%) of these derive from only 3 of 61 known host phyla (Roux et al., 2015a).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numbers from NCBI RefSeq database with citation.

claim: Only 1,531 bacterial and archaeal viruses were entirely sequenced as of the study period.
source: This is because the lack of a universal marker gene for viruses hinders environmental survey capabilities, while the number of isolate viral genomes in databases remains limited: for comparison, more than 25,000 bacterial and archaeal host genomes are available in NCBI RefSeq (January 2015), whereas only 1,531 of their viruses were entirely sequenced and most (86%) of these derive from only 3 of 61 known host phyla (Roux et al., 2015a).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numbers from databases with citation.

claim: 86% of sequenced bacterial and archaeal viruses derive from only 3 of 61 known host phyla.
source: This is because the lack of a universal marker gene for viruses hinders environmental survey capabilities, while the number of isolate viral genomes in databases remains limited: for comparison, more than 25,000 bacterial and archaeal host genomes are available in NCBI RefSeq (January 2015), whereas only 1,531 of their viruses were entirely sequenced and most (86%) of these derive from only 3 of 61 known host phyla (Roux et al., 2015a).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages showing the bias in viral genome representation with citation.

claim: Viral data sets are dominated by 60-95% uncharacterized sequences termed 'viral dark matter'.
source: Thus, although advances in high-throughput sequencing expand the bounds of viral sequence space, these data sets are dominated by uncharacterized sequences (usually 60–95%), termed 'viral dark matter' (Reyes et al., 2012; Youle et al., 2012; Mizuno et al., 2013; Brum and Sullivan, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific range for uncharacterized sequences with multiple citations.

claim: 62% of bacterial genomes tested in early estimations contained at least one prophage.
source: Early estimations, when only a few hundred bacterial genomes were available, suggested that prophages are common (62% of bacterial genomes tested contained at least one), existing as intact and functional forms or in varying degrees of decay (Casjens, 2003).
evidence: The manuscript cites specific percentage from earlier study.

claim: Of the 12,498 sequences, 5,232 were prophages integrated into microbial contigs.
source: Of the 12,498 sequences, 5,232 were prophages (i.e., a viral genome integrated into a microbial contig) and 1,756 were either complete (circularized) or large (>30 kb) genome fragments assembled outside of the host chromosome (i.e., no microbial gene was detected on the contig, Figure 3A, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific counts of prophage sequences.

claim: 1,756 sequences were either complete or large genome fragments assembled outside of the host chromosome.
source: Of the 12,498 sequences, 5,232 were prophages (i.e., a viral genome integrated into a microbial contig) and 1,756 were either complete (circularized) or large (>30 kb) genome fragments assembled outside of the host chromosome (i.e., no microbial gene was detected on the contig, Figure 3A, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific counts of extrachromosomal sequences.

claim: Only 2.3% of large (>30 kb) prophage-originating contigs lacked any identifiable microbial genes in simulations.
source: These analyses suggested that only 2.3% of large (>30 kb) prophage-originating contigs lacked any identifiable microbial genes.
evidence: The manuscript reports results from in silico simulations.

claim: At least 13% of circular and large genome fragments appear to be extrachromosomal prophages based on ParA/ParB genes.
source: These genes were significantly more abundant in the 1,756 circular and large genome fragments than in the rest of the data set (13% vs 1%, respectively; poisson test p-value < 10−05). Thus, at least 13% of these sequences appear to be bona fide extrachromosomal prophages, whereas the others might be lytic viruses in 'carrier' states, chronic infections, or extrachromosomal prophages without detectable ParA/ParB genes.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentage based on statistical analysis of ParA/ParB gene presence.

claim: The VirSorter curated data set improved affiliation by 32% and 40% in Pacific Ocean Viromes and Tara Oceans Viromes, respectively.
source: We found that the VirSorter curated data set improved affiliation by 32 and 40%, respectively, in the marine Pacific Ocean Viromes (POV) (Hurwitz and Sullivan, 2013) and Tara Oceans Viromes (TOV) (Brum et al., 2015) data sets, and more than doubled the number of affiliated genes in human gut viromes (Minot et al., 2012, Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific improvement percentages for different virome datasets with citations.

claim: The VirSorter curated data set more than doubled the number of affiliated genes in human gut viromes.
source: We found that the VirSorter curated data set improved affiliation by 32 and 40%, respectively, in the marine Pacific Ocean Viromes (POV) (Hurwitz and Sullivan, 2013) and Tara Oceans Viromes (TOV) (Brum et al., 2015) data sets, and more than doubled the number of affiliated genes in human gut viromes (Minot et al., 2012, Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific improvement for human gut viromes with citation.

claim: Most (99.3% of 12,498) sequences affiliated to one of 614 virus clusters.
source: Most (99.3% of 12,498) sequences affiliated to one of 614 virus clusters (VCs), of which 535 contained at least one complete genome or large genomic fragment (>30 kb), and approximately half (271 of 535 VCs) included RefSeqABVir sequences (Figure 2A, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages and counts for viral clustering results.

claim: Of 43 RefSeq-curated viral genera, 27 have all their sequences in the same viral cluster.
source: Of 43 RefSeq-curated viral genera, 27 have all their sequences in the same VC, 12 were spread across two VCs, and 4 were spread across >2 VCs—these latter genera included the Spouna-like viruses (3 VCs), N4-like viruses (4 VCs), Lambda-like viruses (9 VCs), and Inoviruses (11 VCs).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific counts showing consistency between VCs and ICTV taxonomy.

claim: Bacterial and archaeal viruses clustered separately in >99% of viral clusters.
source: First, bacterial and archaeal viruses clustered separately in >99% of VCs; the exception (VC_89) included a single and unique (Garrett et al., 2010) archaeal virus (Hyperthermophilic Archaeal Virus 2, NC_014321) that clustered with 21 bacterial viruses, presumably due to poor archaeal virus representation.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentage showing domain-level separation in clustering with citation.

claim: >95% of viral clusters contained exclusively one nucleic acid type.
source: Second, >95% of these VCs contained exclusively one nucleic acid type (e.g., DNA or RNA, and dsDNA or ssDNA, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), although RNA viral representation is low because only RefSeq-curated families Cystoviridae and Leviviridae were available (no RNA viruses were detected with VirSorter, presumably because DNA-based data sets were analyzed).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentage for nucleic acid type consistency in clusters.

claim: Nearly half (2445) of the 5492 microbial genomes with detectable viral signal contained more than one detectable virus.
source: Here, in the 5492 microbial genomes with detectable viral signal, nearly half (2445) contained more than one detectable virus (Figure 4).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific counts for co-infection prevalence.

claim: Approximately 82% of co-infections involved multiple Caudovirales.
source: Most (∼82%) of these co-infections involved multiple Caudovirales, as previously observed (Casjens, 2003), and likely provides mechanism for viral gene exchange and may be more common in some phages displaying rampant mosaicism (e.g., the Siphoviridae, Hendrix et al., 1999) than others.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentage for the most common type of co-infection with citations.

claim: 9% of co-infections occurred between ssDNA Inoviridae and dsDNA Caudovirales.
source: The second most commonly observed co-infections (9%) occurred between ssDNA Inoviridae and dsDNA Caudovirales (Figure 4).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentage for the second most common co-infection type.

claim: The virus-host interaction network displays a modular topology with modularity Q = 0.45.
source: When considering viral diversity at the genus level, the network displays a modular topology (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the network topology with supporting figures showing modularity analysis.

claim: The modularity Q value of 0.45 for the virus-host matrix is significantly higher than randomly permuted matrices (0.02 to 0.17, average 0.07).
source: This virus–host network is detected as significantly modular by lp-Brim (modularity Q = 0.45; the same index computed from 99 randomly permuted matrices ranged from 0.02 to 0.17, with an average of 0.08).
evidence: The figure caption provides specific modularity values and statistical comparison.

claim: Every genome composition metric tested displayed a smaller distance between viruses and their hosts than with non-host genomes.
source: Every metric tested displayed a smaller distance between viruses and their hosts than with non-host genomes, with tetranucleotide frequency (TNF) maximizing the host to non-host distances (Figure 6).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the result of genome composition analysis.

claim: Tetranucleotide frequency (TNF) maximizes the host to non-host distances among all metrics tested.
source: Every metric tested displayed a smaller distance between viruses and their hosts than with non-host genomes, with tetranucleotide frequency (TNF) maximizing the host to non-host distances (Figure 6).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly identifies TNF as the best metric.

claim: Host prediction based on TNF was 99% accurate at both family and genus level for virus-host TNF distances lower than 4×10^-4.
source: When the host database included all host genomes, this host prediction was 99% accurate at both the family and genus level for virus–host TNF distances lower than 4.10−04, 88%/51% (family/genus level) for TNF distances ranging between 4.10−04 and 1.10−03, and 70%/37% for distances greater than 10−03 (Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific accuracy percentages for different distance ranges in Table 1.

claim: VirSorter is designed to predict bacterial and archaeal virus sequences in isolate or single-cell draft genomes, as well as complete genomes.
source: VirSorter is designed to predict bacterial and archaeal virus sequences in isolate or single-cell draft genomes, as well as complete genomes (Roux et al., 2015a).
evidence: The manuscript describes the design and capabilities of VirSorter with citation.

claim: VirSorter identifies viral sequences through statistical enrichment in viral gene content or a combination of viral 'hallmark' genes and viral-like genomic features.
source: Briefly, VirSorter identifies viral sequences through (i) statistical enrichment in viral gene content, using a reference database composed of viral genomes of archaeal and bacterial viruses from RefSeq (hereafter named RefSeqABVir for 'RefSeq Archaea and Bacteria Viruses') and assembled from viral metagenomes (database 'Viromes' in VirSorter), or (ii) a combination of viral 'hallmark' gene(s) that code for virion-related functions such as major capsid proteins or terminases (Koonin et al., 2006; Roux et al., 2014), and at least one viral-like genomic feature: statistical depletion in genes with a hit in the PFAM database, statistical enrichment in uncharacterized genes, short genes, or strand bias (i.e., consecutive genes which tend to be coded on the same strand).
evidence: The manuscript describes the methodology of VirSorter with citations.

claim: The study extended the host range of common viral families to include several recently described phyla like Caldiserica, Marinimicrobia, and Omnitrophica.
source: Simply scanning the identified viruses for novel hosts extended the host range of common viral families to now include several recently described phyla like Caldiserica (formerly known as candidate phylum OP5), Marinimicrobia (SAR406 also known as Marine Group A), or Omnitrophica (OP3), in addition to other understudied groups such as Poribacteria, Nitrospinae, Cloacimonetes (WWE1), and Chloroflexi-type SAR202 (Figure 1, Figure 1—source data 2, Figure 1—source data 3).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly lists the new phyla for which viruses were identified.

claim: Among the unassigned viral group, 7 sequences lacked any hit to a viral reference genome.
source: Among the unassigned group, 7 sequences lacked any hit to a viral reference genome.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific count of sequences without viral reference hits.

claim: The 7 short circular contigs from Bacteroides draft genomes could represent the first complete genomes for an entirely new viral order.
source: If confirmed, these sequences would represent the first complete genomes for an entirely new viral order.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about the potential significance of these sequences.

claim: The false-positive rate in manual curation was 6.7%.
source: Consequently, 892 sequences were discarded (false-positive rate of 6.7%), leaving 12,498 curated sequences.
evidence: The manuscript provides the specific false-positive rate from manual curation.

claim: Extrachromosomal prophages exist outside the microbial chromosome until induced to undergo lytic replication.
source: First, certain types of prophage do not integrate into the host genome. These 'extrachromosomal prophages' (also termed 'plasmid prophage') exist outside the microbial chromosome until induced to undergo lytic replication.
evidence: The manuscript defines extrachromosomal prophages and their behavior.

claim: Extrachromosomal prophages have been known to occur for decades, with coliphage P1 as an example.
source: These have been known to occur for decades (e.g., coliphage P1, Sternberg and Austin, 1981), though their abundance in nature is unknown.
evidence: The manuscript cites historical knowledge of extrachromosomal prophages.

claim: Some phages can enter a 'chronic' cycle in which they replicate outside the host chromosome and produce virions that are extruded without killing their host.
source: Second, some phages can enter a 'chronic' cycle, in which they replicate in the cell outside of the host chromosome, and produce virions that are extruded without killing their host (Abedon, 2009; Rakonjac et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript describes chronic infection cycle with citations.

claim: A phage 'carrier state' has been observed in which a lytic phage is maintained and multiplied within a cultivated host population without measurable effect on cell growth.
source: Third, a phage 'carrier state' has been observed, in which a lytic phage is maintained and multiplied within a cultivated host population without measurable effect on cell growth (Bastías et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript describes the carrier state phenomenon with citation.

claim: Carrier states enabling coexistence of phage and host have been observed in different systems including Vibrio, Escherichia coli, Salmonella, and Flavobacterium.
source: Sometimes also termed 'partial resistance', such states that enable the coexistence of phage and host in culture have now been observed in different systems (Vibrio, Escherichia coli, Salmonella, Flavobacterium), and are linked to slight decreases in growth rate or cell concentration but no host cell clearing as would be observed for 'typical' lytic viruses (i.e., plaque formation), thus could go unnoticed in a microbial cell culture (Fischer et al., 2004; Carey-Smith et al., 2006; Middelboe et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript lists specific systems where carrier states have been observed with citations.

claim: Single amplified genomes are especially valuable for accessing the vast majority of environmental microbes that remain uncultivated in the lab.
source: Finally, single amplified genome (SAG) data sets, sourced from anonymously sorted, amplified, and sequenced cells, are especially valuable for accessing the vast majority of environmental microbes that remain uncultivated in the lab (Rinke et al., 2013; Kashtan et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript describes the value of SAG datasets with citations.

claim: Single-cell amplified genomes can reveal viral sequences directly linked to uncultivated hosts.
source: Single-cell amplified genomes can reveal viral sequences directly linked to uncultivated hosts (Yoon et al., 2011; Roux et al., 2014; Labonté et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript describes the capability of SAGs with citations.

claim: The data set included 4240 complete genomes and 10,547 draft genomes.
source: This data set included 4240 complete genomes and 10,547 draft genomes (as there is no clear annotation of a genome as 'draft' or 'complete' at the NCBI, we identified as 'draft' genomes all genome projects including more than 5 different sequences, to avoid considering genomes split into different chromosomes or including one or several plasmids as 'draft').
evidence: The manuscript provides specific counts of complete and draft genomes analyzed.

claim: VirSorter initially yielded 89,301 total predicted viral sequences from the analyzed genomes.
source: Genomes were processed with VirSorter (Roux et al., 2015a) separately for each class (except for Cyanobacteria, SUP05 SAGs, and the Microbial Dark Matter data set that were all processed together), first using the RefSeqABVir database, and then using the Viromes database, yielding 89,301 total predicted viral sequences.
evidence: The manuscript provides the initial count of predicted sequences before curation.

claim: 938 sequences corresponding to Enterobacteria phage PhiX174 were discarded as they are used for quality control during Illumina sequencing.
source: Among these, 938 correspond to Enterobacteria phage PhiX174, which is used for quality control during Illumina sequencing, and were thus discarded.
evidence: The manuscript explains why certain sequences were removed from the dataset.

claim: Viral clusters (VCs) are approximately equivalent to a RefSeq-curated viral genus.
source: Consistent with previous applications of this method, VCs identified in this analysis were thus approximately equivalent to a RefSeq-curated viral genus (Lima-Mendez et al., 2008b).
evidence: The manuscript states the taxonomic equivalence of VCs with citation.

claim: Host-correlated genome composition patterns were robust across integrated prophages and extrachromosomal genomes among dsDNA viruses.
source: Among dsDNA viruses, host-correlated genome composition patterns were robust across integrated prophages and extrachromosomal genomes (i.e., viral sequences assembled outside of the main host chromosome, Figure 6A, Figure6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the consistency of genome composition patterns across different viral sequence types.

claim: Viral genome composition correlations were strong regardless of the number of viral-encoded tRNA genes.
source: However, these latter expectations were not met as viral and host genome composition correlations were strong regardless of the number of viral-encoded tRNA genes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), which suggests that host-optimized viral genome composition may be beneficial even when the virus encodes its own tRNA genes.
evidence: The manuscript reports unexpected findings about tRNA genes and genome composition with supporting figure.

claim: Among ssDNA viruses, nucleotide composition of viral genomes was correlated to host genomes, but less so than for dsDNA viruses.
source: Among ssDNA viruses, nucleotide composition of viral genomes was also correlated to host genomes, but less so than for dsDNA viruses (Figure 6A).
evidence: The manuscript compares genome composition adaptation between ssDNA and dsDNA viruses.

claim: Microviridae had a reduced signal for genome composition metrics except for codon usage where its signal was comparable to dsDNA viruses.
source: One ssDNA viral group, the Microviridae, had a reduced signal for genome composition metrics except for codon usage where its signal was comparable to that of the dsDNA viruses (Figure 6A).
evidence: The manuscript describes specific patterns for Microviridae.

claim: Inoviridae had reduced genome composition and codon usage adaptation signals.
source: Another ssDNA group, the Inoviridae had reduced genome composition and codon usage adaptation signals.
evidence: The manuscript describes specific patterns for Inoviridae.

claim: Inoviridae release virions without killing their hosts, which may lower selection pressure toward transcription and translation speed and efficiency.
source: Again, because Inoviridae release virions without killing their hosts, it is possible that the virus is exposed to host resources over a much longer time interval, lowering the selection pressure toward transcription and translation speed and efficiency, which is the main mechanism thought to drive genome composition and codon usage adaptation of viral genomes (Cardinale and Duffy, 2011).
evidence: The manuscript provides a mechanistic explanation for Inoviridae patterns with citation.

claim: When genomes from the actual host species are excluded, the accuracy of host prediction drops slightly to 95%, 83%/30%, 67%/30% for the same distance ranges.
source: When genomes from the actual host species are excluded, the accuracy of host prediction drops slightly (95%, 83%/30%, 67%/30% for the same distance ranges), and even more when all genomes from the host genus are excluded (70% and 37% at the family level, no correct genus could be predicted in that case, and only one distance lower than 4.10−04 was observed, Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific accuracy values for different host prediction scenarios in Table 1.

claim: The modular structure of the virus-host interaction network suggests that hosts are specifically associated with particular viruses.
source: Such modularity in virus–host interaction networks suggests that hosts are specifically associated with particular viruses (Weitz et al., 2012), probably reflecting long-term coevolution between microbial hosts and their viruses.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the modularity finding with citation.

claim: Such modular structure was expected but not observed in previous virus-host interaction network studies, likely due to short phylogenetic distances between hosts.
source: Such modular structure was expected, but not observed in previous virus–host interaction network studies, likely due to the short phylogenetic distances between hosts evaluated in available data sets (Flores et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript explains why previous studies did not observe modularity with citation.

claim: The modular network derives from a data set spanning 18 phyla across bacterial and archaeal domains.
source: The modular network presented here derives from a data set spanning 18 phyla across bacterial and archaeal domains.
evidence: The manuscript describes the phylogenetic breadth of the dataset.

claim: The results confirmed the prediction that at macroevolutionary scales, host-phage interaction matrices should be typified by a modular structure.
source: These results confirmed the prediction that 'at macroevolutionary scales, host–phage interaction matrices should be typified by a modular structure' (Flores et al., 2011), as also had been observed across 215 phage types against 286 host types of unknown diversity (Flores et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript confirms a previous prediction with citations.

claim: VirSorter curated data set is made available through two complementary websites: MetaVir and iVirus.
source: To facilitate these follow-up studies, VirSorter curated data set is made available through two complementary websites: MetaVir and iVirus.
evidence: The manuscript describes data availability.

claim: A Data Dryad package including all annotated genbank files from the VirSorter curated data set is available at http://dx.doi.org/10.5061/dryad.b8226.
source: Finally, a summary of the sequences and clusters is provided as Figure 1—source data 1 and Figure 2—source data 1, and a Data Dryad package including all annotated genbank files from the VirSorter curated data set is available (http://dx.doi.org/10.5061/dryad.b8226; Roux et al., 2015b).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific data repository information with citation.

claim: Viruses modulate microbial interaction networks and long-term evolution with resulting feedbacks on ecosystem functions and services.
source: Concomitant with this changing worldview is a growing awareness that viruses modulate microbial interaction networks and long-term evolution with resulting feedbacks on ecosystem functions and services (Suttle, 2007; Rodriguez-Valera et al., 2009; Forterre and Prangishvili, 2013; Hurwitz et al., 2013; Brum et al., 2014; Brum and Sullivan, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript describes the ecological role of viruses with multiple citations.

claim: The lack of a universal marker gene for viruses hinders environmental survey capabilities.
source: This is because the lack of a universal marker gene for viruses hinders environmental survey capabilities, while the number of isolate viral genomes in databases remains limited
evidence: The manuscript identifies a fundamental limitation in viral ecology research.

claim: Interconnected microbial communities drive matter and energy transformations in natural and engineered ecosystems.
source: It is now widely recognized that interconnected microbial communities drive matter and energy transformations in natural and engineered ecosystems (Falkowski et al., 2008), while also contributing to health and disease states in multicellular hosts (Clemente et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript describes the role of microbial communities with citations.

claim: Cultivation-independent molecular methods have profoundly expanded our collective understanding of microbial diversity over the past two decades.
source: Over the past two decades, our collective understanding of microbial diversity has been profoundly expanded by cultivation-independent molecular methods (Pace, 1997; Whitman et al., 1998; Rappé and Giovannoni, 2003; DeLong, 2009; Hanson et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript describes historical progress in microbial ecology with citations.

claim: Numerous tools exist to automatically detect prophages.
source: Numerous tools exist to automatically detect prophages (Fouts, 2006; Lima-Mendez et al., 2008a; Zhou et al., 2011; Akhter et al., 2012), so prophage diversity and abundance are relatively well studied (Casjens, 2003; Canchaya et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript describes available tools for prophage detection with citations.

claim: The VirSorter curated data set includes not only integrated prophage data, but also viruses actively infecting microbes with under-studied infection modes.
source: Finally, both the detection of non-integrated viral genomes and the improved virome affiliation suggest that the VirSorter curated data set includes not only integrated prophage data, but also viruses actively infecting these microbes (i.e., not integrated in the host chromosome and producing virions) with under-studied infection modes.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the composition of the dataset based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: Co-infection by multiple viruses appears common based on the data.
source: Together, these findings suggest that genome-based network analyses could be used to identify novel viruses, as well as to infer host domain (archaeal or bacterial, >99% accuracy) and nucleic acid type (ssDNA or dsDNA, >95% accuracy). Evolutionarily, we posit that while co-infection by multiple viruses appears common, the consistency of so many VCs with ICTV taxonomy suggests that most phage genomes harbor a largely vertically inherited core gene set
evidence: The manuscript draws conclusions about co-infection prevalence from the data.

claim: Most phage genomes harbor a largely vertically inherited core gene set rather than rampant mosaicism.
source: Evolutionarily, we posit that while co-infection by multiple viruses appears common, the consistency of so many VCs with ICTV taxonomy suggests that most phage genomes harbor a largely vertically inherited core gene set as detected for marine T4-like populations (Ignacio-Espinoza and Sullivan, 2012; Marston et al., 2012; Deng et al., 2014) rather than the rampant mosaicism paradigm largely derived from Siphoviridae genomes (Hendrix et al., 1999).
evidence: The manuscript proposes an evolutionary interpretation based on the clustering results with citations.

claim: Horizontal gene transfer may be more prevalent in phages that occupy host cells longer due to lysogenic or chronic infection stages and/or infect densely packed hosts.
source: Specifically, we posit that horizontal gene transfer is more prevalent in phages that occupy host cells longer due to lysogenic or chronic infection stages and/or infect densely packed hosts (e.g., biofilms or clumped life stages) as these parameters would increase the probability of co-infection.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a hypothesis about factors influencing horizontal gene transfer.

claim: For highly lytic viral groups, genome-based clustering approaches can be leveraged for their taxonomic predictive value.
source: Perhaps then, at least for more highly lytic viral groups, genome-based clustering approaches can now be leveraged for their taxonomic predictive value as suggested over a decade ago (Rohwer and Edwards, 2002).
evidence: The manuscript proposes a practical application based on the findings with citation.

claim: The mining of publicly available microbial genomic data proved to be a useful complement to other virus-host linkage approaches.
source: Here, the mining of publicly available microbial genomic data proved to be a useful complement to these approaches as it enables the exploration of host-linked viral diversity.
evidence: The manuscript concludes about the value of the approach used.

claim: The current VirSorter data set remains limited by the cultivation bias inherent in publicly available complete and draft microbial genomes.
source: While this current VirSorter data set remains limited by the cultivation bias inherent in the publicly available complete and draft microbial genomes, such bias will progressively be eliminated as SAGs are used to better map microbial dark matter (e.g., Rinke et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges limitations of the current dataset with citation.

claim: A drastically improved map of the virosphere will help reveal the eco-evolutionary forces shaping virus-host interactions across diverse ecosystems.
source: Such a drastically improved map of the virosphere, together with advances in experimental approaches and theory (Brum and Sullivan, 2015), will help reveal the eco-evolutionary forces shaping virus–host interactions across diverse ecosystems and eventually shift our inference capability from observation to prediction.
evidence: The manuscript discusses future implications with citation.
